title: Who really built the pyramids?
subtitle: Neither slaves nor aliens
subject: histoire
description: Slaves, Atlanteans or aliens: everything has been said about the builders of Giza. A 4,500-year-old logbook and a workers' town dug out of the sand finally give the answer.
author: ezgi-gizem-berkay

hero.hook: Copper tools, rope and nearly six million tons of stone: an inspector's logbook finally tells who did the work.

blocks.text: For **forty-five centuries**, the pyramids of Giza have stood in plain sight. And for almost as long, people have asked who built them. The answers range from romantic daydreams to conspiracy theories: aliens, Atlanteans, a lost civilization. All of them start from the same idea: without modern machines, humans could never have pulled it off.

Yet the pyramids are **royal tombs**, designed as gateways to the afterlife, where the pharaoh begins his eternal reign. They were planned and executed with a care and precision that matched that purpose. And since the discovery of the papyri of an inspector named [[Merer]], the question of "who" has largely been answered.

sections.title: Khufu's building site: two million blocks

blocks.text: The Great Pyramid was raised for the pharaoh [[Khufu]]. It contains more than **two million** stone blocks, each weighing between two and fifteen tons. For the burial chamber, granite beams weighing up to **80 tons** were hauled from [[Aswan]], 900 kilometers to the south. At about **146 meters**, it towered over the whole plateau.

blocks.caption: The mastaba of Iteti in the eastern necropolis at Giza, excavated by Schiaparelli in 1903, with the pyramids behind.

blocks.text: The Great Pyramid remained the tallest structure on the planet for close to four thousand years.

A project like this required a large, well-supplied workforce: tens of thousands of men, in crews that rotated through the site. To house and feed them, a town of some **seven hectares** was built for the purpose at the foot of the [[Giza Plateau]]. Films and novels long pictured slaves driven to the work. The people who actually built the pyramid were free Egyptians.

sections.title: Merer's diary and the workers' town

blocks.text: For a long time, nobody knew how the work was organized. In **2013**, a French team excavating [[Wadi al-Jarf]], an ancient harbor on the Red Sea, uncovered the oldest inscribed papyri ever found in Egypt, sealed in a gallery cut into the rock. They were the logbooks of Merer, a mid-level inspector.

Day after day, Merer recorded the work of his crew of about forty men, part of a larger team of roughly **two hundred**. Their job: to sail down the Nile with fine limestone from the quarries at [[Tura]] to Giza, for the outer casing that made the pyramid gleam. Two or three round trips every Egyptian ten-day week.

The other half of the picture came out of the ground beside the plateau. Since **1988**, the archaeologist [[Mark Lehner]] has been excavating the workers' town. It dates mainly to the reigns of Khufu's successors, Khafre and Menkaure, and shows workers who were housed and well cared for.

Feeding a workforce of roughly **ten thousand** was an enormous undertaking. By one estimate, about **eleven cattle** and **thirty-seven sheep or goats** were slaughtered every day, on top of large quantities of grain, bread, beer and fish. The sheer amount of pottery recovered is itself a sign of a large, well-provisioned settlement.
The menu also included dates, olive oil and honey: prized foods that are hard to picture being served to slaves.

Archaeologists also identified the outline of long galleries about **35 meters** in length, with thick walls supporting a flat roof, arranged side by side. Each could hold about forty people, close to the size of Merer's crew. An efficient way to house a large workforce.

sections.title: A vanished branch of the Nile and a lot of engineering

blocks.text: Giza was chosen first of all because **limestone** was abundant there. Canals were dug and harbors built to bring the blocks by water from the Nile to the foot of the site. The workers also carved and leveled the base of the Great Pyramid straight out of the natural rock.

blocks.caption: Satellite view: the pyramids at the edge of the desert, the green Nile Valley and Cairo right next door.

blocks.text: Some **4,500 years ago**, the plateau was greener and wetter than it is today. A western branch of the Nile, since vanished, ran close enough to float the heavy stone almost to the building site. Animals may have helped pull the loads. But the only "secret power" behind the pyramids was engineering and human labor.

blocks.text: Neither aliens nor a lost civilization: the pyramids are the work of free, skilled, well-fed Egyptians, with their own quarters, food and trades. Their only secret was engineering.
